utterances.text: I mean the population, non-Serb population. I mean the Muslims. Even women had to perform labour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And what sort of work was your son doing? What sort of tasks was he given?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: He had to go and dig trenches in Gradacac. Palata Sacir and Odobasic got killed then. He was wounded. He fell. He was collapsed and then he was brought back to Samac and then he was spared from work for a while, and later on worked in the post office.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: When you say "he was wounded," are you referring to one of those two men that you mentioned, Palata and the other gentleman, Odobasic?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: They were killed. Sacir and Odobasic. Sacir was a teacher or something like that. He worked in education.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Who was wounded?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: My son was not wounded. He simply fell. He slipped, out of fear, or just collapsed, and then he was brought home and stayed in bed for a few days. And then Stevo told him to go with him. The cow was confiscated and taken to the field in Pisari and then he worked there. They didn't abuse him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. Let's just take it a bit more slowly so that we can make sure we all understand what you're saying. The place that your son --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Page 49, line 24, after the word "abused him" and then full stop, I believe that witness said: "And he was feeling well then, he was in good condition there." So maybe just for the sake of transcript we can clarify that, because the witness added something after these words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. MR. DI FAZIO: Certainly. I'll clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: After your son was taken to the fields in Pisari and worked there, did he -- was he in better or in good health condition?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Let's go back to the period of time when he was in Gradacac and working on trenches. Did he ever report to you that he was digging trenches in Gradacac at the same time that combat was going on?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I want to turn to the sequence of events leading to your arrest. You've told us that you were arrested on the 23rd of May, 1992, but in fact I want to ask you about an episode that occurred before that. Do you know a man named Pero Kitic or Katic?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Pero Kitic. He was a chess player, a friend of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Incidentally, just let's diverge there. Were you a well-known chess player in Bosnia prior to April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you play competitively and at a fairly high level?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Let's turn to this man Kitic, Pero Kitic. Did he ever come to your house following the 16th -- the events of the 16th and 17th of April?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. He played chess. There was a competition, memorial competition, in the memorial hall. Dragan Jokanovic and chess players from all over Yugoslavia, Croatia, Macedonia, used to come, from all over former Yugoslavia. Pero Kitic stayed in my house, together with seven other people. At the time he lived in Vukovar and worked there, although originally he was from Bosnia, but I can't remember the name of the village. He was a very nice man.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thank you. But I'm now talking about events following the 16th and 17th of April, after that, those dates. Did he come to your house?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Who was he with, if anyone?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: He came with Fadil Topcagic. There was a Ford vehicle there, Ford Tranzit vehicle. Fadil knocked on the door and my wife went to open the door and came to tell me that they wanted to see me. I went out into the yard. Pero Kitic stepped out of the vehicle and said to Fadil, "You carry on with the list. I know Kemal, and I cannot take him with me." So he basically saved my skin then. He was a Serb by ethnicity, but he was a good man.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you actually recall reference to a list?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: I don't know which list you mean. Is it the list pertaining to people being taken away?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to identify any list or anything like that. All I'm interested in knowing is: Did Pero Kitic, when he told Topcagic not to take you, did he refer to a list of some sort?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. He said, "You carry on according to the list." And they went on. He came into the house with me. He knew Biba's name; he knew her by her name. He greeted us. He sat down. We started eating. And he told me, "Kemal, don't leave the house. The war is going on. There are many paramilitaries here in Samac, so just remain where you are. I will be here." That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And was Topcagic a member of the 4th Detachment, as far as you're aware?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you anyone who was in the 4th Detachment just because I don't know for sure. I don't know who was a member of the 4th Detachment. I know that Simo was the commander of the 4th Detachment, and now, as to the people who were members, I don't know. What I just told you, I know based on my previous knowledge of the party. It was associated with the party movement for Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's turn now to the events of the 23rd of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me. I wonder whether, Mr. Bobic, you could just briefly elaborate. You say, in response to Mr. Di Fazio's question concerning the 4th Detachment that you don't know who was a member of the 4th Detachment, but then you go on to say that Simo was the commander of the 4th Detachment. I wonder whether you could tell us, first of all, Simo who; and secondly, how did you know that this person was the commander of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was widely known in Samac. They knew who was the president of the HDZ. It was somebody named Nujic. We knew who was the president of the municipality. Izet Izetbegovic was the president of our party, the SDA, and then Sulejman Tihic came. Mr. Boro Pisarevic was the president of the SDP, and Mesud Nogic. These were the parties that existed. There was a youth party, president of MOS was my son, as I have told you previously. It was all known. There was the SDS party, which I didn't mention. I can't tell you who was the member of the 4th Detachment and who was the member of the SDS, because I think that that was identical. That's all I have to say. I can't claim, but I think that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Bobic, but my question was specific. You mention that somebody called Simo was the commander of the 4th Detachment, and my question is: Simo who? What is the surname? And secondly, how you knew that this person was the commander of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Simo Zaric was the commander of the 4th Detachment. Many Muslims used to come to my shop. Many of them who were members of the 4th Detachment. There were a lot of Muslims in Simo Zaric's unit. This is common knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I'm allowed. I mean, we all heard this witness speaking in our language, when using the term "president of the 4th Detachment"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Literally, he said "president." And in the transcript we have noticed that the word "commander" was used. Because this witness was testifying about certain links within certain political party, and we are not 100 per cent sure that he's using correct words for detachment and the party. So maybe this could be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sure Mr. Di Fazio can clarify that with the witness. MR. DI FAZIO: If it's a question of translation, certainly I'll do that, but of course someone may refer to someone as being a president of a body even though someone might use a different term. But I'll clarify that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Just tell us again how you regarded Simo Zaric's role in the 4th Detachment. Did you regard him as the president of that body or the commander of that body?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: He was something of a commander, commander of the 4th Detachment. I'm not fully sure, and I apologise if I made any mistakes. At the time, all political parties were legal, so that I don't see any issue there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And you haven't made any mistakes. Did you ever see Simo Zaric engaged in any activity, doing anything or saying anything, that indicated to you his role in the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go now to the 23rd of May, 1992, the day of your arrest. Did men come to your house?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. They came on the 23rd of May. Naser Sejdic came, with two other men whom I didn't know. They came by foot, because my house was close to the SUP building. I lived in Ivo Lola Ribar Street, and the SUP building was in Marsala Tito Street. They told me -- Naser told me that I had to go to the SUP building because Simo Zaric had ordered me to be taken in for an informative interview. So he told me -- they told me that, and I went there on foot. And as I got there, he was there in the office. Savo Djordjevic was there, a former policeman from Rijeka. He told me, "Go into the room." I entered the room, and then he told me, "Kemal," he had already known my name, "Kemal, empty your pockets." And I took out everything. I had a handkerchief there, money, my shop keys. And he told me, "Just leave it all there." So I put it on the desk. And then he said, "Take off your shoelaces." So I took shoelaces out of both of my shoes. I put it on the desk as well. And then he told me, "Go on. You can go either down into the yard or to the room across the corridor." So I went to that room that was across from the toilet. And as I entered that room, I saw people in there, and I asked them what was going on. And then Zlatko Stanic, the director of the electrical power company, a wonderful man, told me, "Kemal, just keep quiet." And I kept quiet. Mato Matok was there, Ahmed Coralic, Mirsad Cosic, and then a man with the last name of Pelesevic. I can't remember his first name. All in all, there were 12 or 15 of us. So I was in that room that was previously used for issuing IDs and passports. And then a young man of a very large build came in --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can I ask you just to pause there? Thank you. We've got the picture now and I just want to clarify one or two aspects about that answer. First of all, the man who came to the house to get you in the first place, Naser Sejdic, what ethnic background was he?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Naser Sejdic, yes. He was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you know if he -- I withdraw that question. Thank you. And the men whose names you just read out in that last answer, who were in the room that you were -- that you entered, what ethnic background were they?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Croats and Muslims. Stanic was a Croat, Mato Matok was a Croat, and there were a number of Muslims there. It's been a long time, ten or eleven years, so I can't remember it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes, but all I want to know is this: Were they Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: They were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thanks. And the other man you mentioned who greeted you when you first arrived, Savo Djordjevic, I believe his name was, was he of Serbian ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. He is a former policeman from Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Where is Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks. Now, let's go back to the room in which you were kept. Were you eventually taken from that room to somewhere else in the SUP building?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. A man came whom, as I will later find out, was the bodyguard of Stevan Todorovic, so he came in. And he said, "Who is new here?" I said I was, and he said, "Come upstairs," so I came upstairs, and they told me it was going to be an informative interview and this is how they got us to come to SUP. They tricked us, in fact. And then they told me -- I was about to sit down, and then Stiv said, "No, no, no," and then he started hitting me with a baton on my face and then my eye, you can still see, is a bit smaller. He started hitting me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I'm going to get you to give details of that in a moment, but before you get there, there's some questions I'd like to ask you. First of all, the condition -- I forgot to ask you the condition of the men in the room downstairs, the men who you described, the Muslims and Croats who you were with. Had they been beaten or attacked on this occasion, or did they appear to be physically in reasonable condition?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: They were intimidated. Some of them had been beaten, not all of them. They were afraid, which is natural. The war was on. If they brought you to the SUP building, that means that people had reason to be afraid, because they had done nothing wrong but were brought there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now let's turn back to the room in which Todorovic started to beat you. First of all, can you tell us the names of everyone who was in the room at that time?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: All right. There was Stevan Todorovic, Stiv; then there was Perica Krstanovic; and Predrag Adzic and also Stiv's bodyguard. Stiv beat me up there just as I started telling you a minute ago. He kicked me with his shoes some 10 to 12 times. I fell down. And then he hit me in my chest. And I started -- the blood started coming out. And he told me to wipe it, and I wiped it with my sweater. I wiped the blood. And then he said, "Take him downstairs." I came downstairs, and the people in the room came to my assistance immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go back to the beating. First of all, did Todorovic use any instruments?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. He hit me with a baton which was about 20 centimetres long, directly in my eye, and I still can't see very well in that eye. I was all blue and bruised.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Which eye?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Here, in my left eye.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: You can see that it's smaller.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Is that the result -- that disability, the fact that it's smaller, a consequence of the beating that you suffered at the hands of Todorovic on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And in addition to it being smaller, can you actually see with that eye very well?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: I can see in a certain percentage. When I went to the retirement commission, they told me that my eyesight was 60 per cent worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Right. Put very simply, did the beating and the blow that you received to your eye not only make your eye look smaller, but did it actually affect the vision? That's all I want to know.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes, naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. You also said that you had to clean the blood that you were spitting up. Clean it from where?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Off the desk, his desk -- I mean Stiv's desk, because that's where everything was happening, in his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did the others come to your aid or do anything to try to restrain him or control him?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: No. No. They just looked on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. You were taken downstairs?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. Then Stiv ordered me to be taken downstairs. The people in the room downstairs gave me aid, gave me some water, and wiped off the blood with a bandanna. And then as I leaned against the wall to rest, the bodyguard of Stevan Todorovic came and said, "Bobic, you're wanted upstairs again." When I got up there, Simo Zaric was sitting there, probably to see what I looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when you say when you got up there, what room are you talking about? Was it the same room in which you had been attacked by Todorovic or was it a different room?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: The same room where I had been beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Where Stevo beat me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And who was present in the room? Go through the names, please.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Stevan Todorovic was up there; so was Simo Zaric now, he was there too; Predrag Adzic, Taso's son; and Perica Krstanovic, Zivko's son was up there. They called him in to -- so that he was -- would be able to see what I looked like, and when he saw me, he laughed ironically, and Todorovic said, "Take him down, downstairs." They didn't beat me any more. I went downstairs and the man on the staircase told me, "You got off lightly."

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do I take it from your answer that you did not hear Mr. Zaric actually say anything in the room other than the laughter that you've referred to, the ironic laughter that you referred to, you didn't hear him say anything. Is that the situation?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: No. No, he didn't say anything to me. He knows very well that this is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thanks. How long did you remain in the SUP building in custody?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: I was in the SUP building from the 23rd of May until the 28th of June, when I was transferred to the TO building, across the road from SUP, because the Territorial Defence building had its premises there. So I was transferred to a larger room there. There were two rooms there, quite big, and that's where we were transferred. We slept in the area where weapons had been kept before. It was some kind of a large bed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm interested in the period of time in which you were in custody in the SUP building, and I'm now concentrating on that, not the TO, okay? So you're in the SUP until 28th of June, 1992. In that period of time, did more and more prisoners keep coming in, being kept at the SUP?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes, they kept bringing them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Of what ethnic background were these people?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did they endure beatings?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you comment on the frequency with which beatings were inflicted in the SUP in that period of time, that month up to the 28th of June?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Do you mean as far as I'm concerned, when I was transferred to the TO, from the 28th of June onwards? Because I explained that I was transferred to --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I'm concentrating on the SUP. Keep your mind focused on the SUP building, okay, up until the 28th -- we'll get to the TO later, all right? Now, in that period of time that you were in the SUP, can you comment on the frequency of beatings? And that applies to you, if you were beaten, but also to any other beatings that any other prisoners suffered. I want to know if it was a frequent occurrence, a rare occurrence, whether it occurred daily, if so, how often, whether it occurred only at night, whether it occurred in the day, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: People were taken out every day. We were in this room that I have already described, where passports and ID cards used to be issued. And we saw all the people who were taken to SUP and those who left SUP. It was possible to see out, because there were some transparent openings there. And every day somebody was brought in, and after a while the room became too crowded. Nobody could fit in any more. There was a desk there. There was also a filing cabinet for ID cards, and also some other items where the forms for ID cards and passports were kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. We'll get to the living conditions in a moment, but let's get first to the beatings. Can you comment on the frequency of beatings in the SUP in that month?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't see that, but one could only hear the screams. And when we went to the toilet, the corridor was quite short and narrow, as this desk, and there were rooms on both sides of the corridor, and you could see blood on the wall. We heard everything. We heard the screams when people were beaten, people from -- that's what we heard from our room. But I didn't see it. I didn't see who beat them, how they were beaten. But the people who conducted the beatings were always the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. Thank you for clarifying that. How often would you hear the screams? How often would you hear the screams of people being beaten?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: It was quite often, and people could hear it even from Slavonia, because the SUP building was quite close to the Sava River, and that's how I heard later on that people in Orasje heard it. Even when I was beaten they heard it. This was done mostly at night. They would come in drunk and they would beat people. They were led by Stevo Todorovic. That was the select company.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that it occurred mostly at night. Did you ever hear the screams resulting from beatings during the day?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: To a lesser extent. Perhaps sometimes, but it was not as strong, because people were also brought in at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. In the limited travel that you had in the building, in the actual inside of the building, in that month, did you see blood on walls wherever you went or was it only in certain locations?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: In a certain location in the corridor down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thanks. Now let's -- can you tell the Chamber about the living conditions that you had in that month up to your transfer to the TO? First of all, food and water. What sort of food did you get, how often, and what about water?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: We did have water. We hardly received any food at all. We would receive some tea once a day, and that was one cup for two people, just a few sips for each of us. And we would also receive a very thin slice of white bread. We would be given this around noon and as soon as we ate they came in to beat us. The beatings followed immediately afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What about sleeping conditions? Were you provided with anywhere to lie down, anything to keep warm at night, blankets, pillows, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: In SUP we were not given anything. We couldn't really sleep. How could one sleep when people would be brought in from their work every day? So that we just stood there. You couldn't -- you didn't have enough room even to sit down any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Now, you said that you were transferred to the TO building on the 28th of June. Everyone knows that that's just across the road from the SUP. But before we get on to what happened in the SUP, I want to ask you this question: Up until the 28th of June, had anyone explained to you why you had been arrested, what it was that you had done wrong to cause you to be locked up in this room at the SUP?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: No one did. No. We were just brought there, myself and all the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Let's turn our attention now to the TO. You were transferred there on the 28th of June, 1992, and on the 3rd of July -- just answer me yes or no. Just answer me yes or no: On the 3rd of July, were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Very well. I'll return to the issue of that particular episode later, but first of all, I want you to tell the Chamber of the conditions in the -- generally that existed in the TO. Did other men suffer beatings?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. They beat people every day. A German by the name of Inger [phoen] was with me. There was the parish priest, Jozo Puskaric. He served in Croatia and from Hrvatska Tisina. And also there were some other 11 Croatian lads who were beaten from Hrvatska Tisina. Zvaka Rakic beat them, Spasoje Bogdanovic, Sole, Slobodan Jacimovic, Slavko Trivunovic. That was the team that beat them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: These names that you have just mentioned, were they local men or men from surrounding towns and villages?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. Slobodan Jacimovic is from Batkusa, the others were from Skarici. There's this guy by the name of Krezo Makso Teodorovic, father's name Isailo. He's also from Batkusa. He brought in the people from Serbia to beat us. He invented all kinds of things; that I didn't like Serbs, and then they would beat me; that the parish priest had raped a Serb child aged 7, and then Lugar and the others would beat the parish priest. And also the 11 guys outside. And scenes like this just kept being repeated.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: That's what I want to know. You say scenes like this kept being repeated. Was it a daily occurrence that attacks of this nature took place?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. It happened also during the day and during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did the men who were attacked scream and cry out loudly during their beatings?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were they beaten and did they scream and cry out loudly in the courtyard of the TO building?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What was the ethnic background of the men who were imprisoned in. TO building?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Muslims and Croats. Jozo Puskaric was a Croat. He was the parish priest. And there was also this German guy by the name of Jurgen. I think his last name was Janke, Jurgen Janke.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was he a truck driver who found himself inside?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was heading for Gradacac and then in Pelagicevo they stopped him and made him return to Samac. His truck was parked in front of the SUP. I wouldn't have been able to understand him, but Esef Zaimovic [As interpreted] spoke fluent German and we were able to speak to him. Esef Zaimbegovic [As interpreted] was a manager in Uniglas, which was a German company.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. How long did you remain in the TO altogether?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: I was there from the 28th, and then the night that they transferred us to Batkovici, I think it was on the 11th of October, as far as I can remember. They took us to Batkovici with our eyes tied, with blindfolds, and we went on two buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. Now let's remain with the TO building, and remember that I'm going to come back to your individual -- the beating that you suffered on the 3rd of July later. I'm now talking about what you saw happened to other men, okay? The beatings that you've described, were instruments used?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. Baseball bats, and also batons, but not the standard-issue police batons, but really big ones. Then parts of chairs. They brought in all kinds of planks. And then we would see -- as we walked around, we saw a military small truck, TAM, and we saw everything on that truck. So we couldn't sleep at night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: And then they took us out.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, page 65, line 25, it says on the 11th of October. I think that the witness said on the 11th or on the 10th. So could we just clarify whether he did mention the month at all, and what month he thinks that they were brought in. Because I understood him to have said "on the 11th or on the 10th." Could this be clarified with the witness, please. MR. DI FAZIO: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Just so we can be clear about what was actually interpreted to us,

utterances.speaker: MR. BOBIC
utterances.text: Did you say that you were transferred to Batkovici on the 10th or 11th of October? Was that your answer?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: I think it was in November. It's either on the 11th of October or on the 10th of November. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Don't bother referring to material, Mr. Bobic. It's okay. I'm happy with your answer. It was later in the year, October or November, you were transferred to Batkovici. That will do me fine. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did men in the TO ever have their teeth pulled?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You suffered that fate, I believe.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: We'll get to it later. What about other men? Did you see other men having their teeth pulled?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did anyone in particular engage in that activity, or was it more than one person?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: That was Slavko Trivunovic. His nickname was Zubar, dentist. It was a well-known fact. He pulled people's teeth out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were people forced to sing songs?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. Every night we sang songs, "From Topola to Ravna Gora," "General Draza's Guards are Everywhere." And if somebody used the word "djeneral" instead of "general," then he would be beaten. They also had to sing some other songs and then they would single out a soldier -- I'm sorry -- they would single out one of the prisoners, give him a baton, and then he would have to act as a conductor in a way. That was the way it was done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, I think we're going into the details which are not contested by the Defence, as you know, the ill-treatment in those places. MR. DI FAZIO: I've just about wrapped that up, if Your Honours please. I'm now going to go to the specific beating. And following that, when I go to Batkovici, there will be virtually just a very brief overview of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, but I think we've wasted some time on the details of matters not contested by the Defence. This has been cleared already. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Well, I don't intend to go into the matters generally any further, if Your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The beating that you suffered in particular on the 3rd of July, who inflicted that upon you, and what time was it?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: It was at night. It was at 1.00 a.m. Stevan Todorovic, Stiv, was there; so was Slavko Trifunovic; Slobodan Jacimovic; Slobodan Rakic, nicknamed Zvaka; Spaso Bogdanovic, called Sole; Tubonja; Savo Cancarevic. I can't remember all the names. There were quite a few of them. There were also people from the outside, not the locals, people from Serbia, whom I didn't know. They came to beat me that night because a man by the name of Kapija had died. He was killed in the war. And whenever something like that happened, if a Serb got killed, they would come to the camp and beat us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in the course of the attack that you suffered that night, were you struck with a rifle?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. Bobo Radulovic was there. I didn't mention him. He was a former police officer in Odzak. Boban Radulovic, nicknamed Bobo, from Skarici, he worked as a police officer in Odzak; he and Jacimovic started beating me right away. And I said Slobodan, "Don't beat me." And Bobo said, "Hit him. You know -- you see that he knows your name." So he first struck me in the head, here, and I had a really big gash here. And one could see my skull, because the skin just collapsed. And later on they had to put stitches. They broke both of my arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me direct you to what I want from this episode, okay? Just the injury that you suffered to your skull. You can see now visibly, quite clearly, a deep scar that you have across your forehead, about three inches long, quite visible, quite deep. Is that as a result of the blow that you suffered with a rifle butt?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Were cigarettes extinguished in your mouth?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you have a nail driven into your leg just below the knee?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you still have a scar as a result of the nail being hammered into your leg? You need to say yes or no so it's recorded. I can't hear you.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I've seen the scar that he bears on his leg as a result of the nail being driven in. Do you want the witness to show it to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Is there any contest? MR. DI FAZIO: I don't think there will be any contest, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, it's not necessary. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You can just describe what -- just briefly. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was your leg broken?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was fractured, but not fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Subsequently --

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: -- down there, on my right leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Subsequently, in the United States, did you have to have metal plate and pins put into your leg at the site of that injury?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: No. They didn't put it on my leg, but I had surgery on my left arm, here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes. I'll get to your arms in a moment. I may be wrong about the metal plate. Is it the case that you've only got the metal plates in your arms, not your leg?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Just on my left arm, here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: That's where I had the surgery in the States.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Were both of your forearms broken?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. Here. I have pins all over this arm here. MR. DI FAZIO: For the purposes of the record, if Your Honours please, the witness demonstrates -- shows us his forearms and the visible scars on the forearms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did they, in attacking you, use a heavy metal spring, baseball bats, other instruments?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And were your teeth pulled from your jaw, healthy teeth, pulled out of your jaw that night?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. Four of my teeth were pulled out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And I think you were fortunate enough to faint and lose consciousness at some stage during this onslaught. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have a break for 20 minutes? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We'll continue our proceedings at 1250 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution is continuing. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I want to turn now to your transfer to Batkovici. You've said that took place in October or November of 1992. In Batkovici, did you suffer the same sort of conditions as had existed in the SUP and TO, or were things better there?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: After we started from Samac to Batkovici, Savo Sofrenovic entered the bus and told us that he had a difficult duty to perform. He gave us white blindfolds to cover our eyes. I saw on my bus a man called Zvaka, Slobodan Rakic, Zvaka, and Rakic Miroslav, who were both armed, and they escorted us all the way to Batkovici. Savo told us to put the blindfold on our eyes, that we were not allowed to look around as we were travelling. Prior to that, women and children came to see us. They cried. We had to leave and they remained there. I told my wife to go home, and then the bus started, headed to Batkovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: We came to Batkovici --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you for that. Let me ask you this: When were you eventually exchanged in Sarajevo? What was the date?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: It was on the 6th of October, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Would Your Honours just bear with me for a moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, on Batkovici, you did ask about the conditions. There was no answer. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, I know. I'm going to get to that. I was getting the time frame first, and I'll get on to the conditions now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So about almost two years in Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's get back to the conditions that you saw and experienced in Batkovici. Compared to the TO and the SUP, what was it like there?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: It was a bit better in Batkovici. We weren't afraid as much. We felt a bit relieved. We went to work every day. When we came to Batkovici, and before we entered the premises, I saw that it was a typical camp with a wire around it. There were hangars there. We were standing out in the freezing rain. And then the commander of the camp, whose name I don't know, came. He left soon afterwards. So he took us in and he said that we were in the Batkovici collection or holding centre, and he told us that for any disobedience or refusal to carry out tasks, we would be killed and abused. He warned us not to try to escape. This is how it was in that camp. We were lined in four lines. They started calling out names in an alphabet order. Since my last name started with B, I was among the first ones whose names were called out. There were two soldiers standing at the door. I didn't know those two soldiers. But as we entered, the soldiers hit us with their hands and kicked us in our bottoms. When I came in, I found that 20 young Muslims from Bijeljina who had refused to join the army, and they were brought there for 20 days, pursuant to the order of the misdemeanour judge. This is how they explained it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to ask you, though, to describe conditions generally, not bit by bit. Just over the two-year period that you were in Batkovici, can you inform the Chamber of the sort of conditions that you had? Perhaps you can tell us first of your sleeping conditions, what you had, if anything; and secondly, any food and so on. And just be brief about it. We just want a quick overview, a quick picture of it.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: We slept on cement floor and we had some hay. We had nothing to cover us with. These were huge hangars, they were very drafty, and they were originally intended for grain.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Just a small detail. While the witness stayed there for almost two years, what was the temperature during different times of the year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was unbearable. Hangars were quite high, and they had thin wooden boards covering the ceiling, and sometimes the temperature would climb quite high. We had a barrel split in half in which we urinated, and that also contributed to the increased temperature, and there was a very unpleasant stench inside. We were not able to wash ourselves. We had no facilities for washing. Only sometimes we would get some cold water.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: What about the winter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a bit better in wintertime, because in the meantime the ICRC had come, and they registered us in November, so they knew that we were there. Some people were exchanged, and those of us who remained received blankets, clothes, coffee, sugar, cigarettes. But later on they would take it away from us in the camp, so it wasn't really of much use to us. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: One of the answers that you -- one of the matters raised in your last answer is that you were registered in November by the ICRC. Can you recall, November of what year? Was it 1992 or 1993, or indeed 1994 -- sorry, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So very soon after your arrival at Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, had you had any contact with the ICRC previously at all?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. In Bosanski Samac, in the SUP building, there was the Serb Red Cross, not the international one. And a woman - I can't remember her name, but she was the wife of Savo Petkovic - came, and she registered all of us, entered our names in a notebook, and she came with another man. I don't know him. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm actually more concerned about the International Committee for the Red Cross. Did they -- did you ever have any contact with them prior to being transferred to Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: No, we had no contact. They were looking for us in Samac, but they couldn't find us there. And then some woman from Zasavica told them that we were in the SUP and the TO buildings. I think her last name is Porobic and the first name is Suhra. She told them where we were. And then the International Red Cross Committee started searching for us and exerting pressure, as a result of which they had to transfer us to Batkovici once the exchanges started. That was a central camp, a typical sort of camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Just while we're on this topic: Did you ever see or hear of representatives of the ICRC coming into either the SUP or the TO buildings?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: No. They were never there, because they were not allowed. They had no access to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. In the TO, was there a guard room close by?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. Once you go through the room, there was the toilet nearby, but we were not used -- we were not allowed to use that toilet frequently because they would beat us on our way there. So we frequently had to use old plastic bags to relieve ourselves in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. But the guard room, was that ever used for any other purpose?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: It was used for their purposes, the guards who guarded us were there. It was a well-furnished room. It had military-style iron beds. And when the Red Cross came, they would go to that room. And then sometimes -- somebody told me that the Red Cross was there, but we were presented to them as Serbs so that they would get a good impression, and they would take people to that room to meet with them. It's a small room with some four beds.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you know which Red Cross would meet people in the room? Was it the local Red Cross or the International Committee of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was probably the international one. These ladies, the International Red Cross, was looking for us. They learned of us in Zasavica. It's a Catholic village near Crkvina. And they turned that Catholic village into a camp, a typical women camp. However, they called it the collection centre. Many women were registered there. Many women had to go and work in Odzak, in Modrica, go plum-picking, potato digging, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, something that we heard here in the transcript, on page 76, line 9. It says: "Somebody told me." And we believe that we heard certain name of a person who told him about that. So maybe my colleague can clarify that. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. I'd be grateful to you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Who told you that the Red Cross was there in the guard room?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: It was Tihic Pasaga, son of Smail, and Fetisa's [phoen] Son, who will later be killed in the TO building. And there were a few other Muslims who had been arrested there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And you commented that: "We were presented to them," that is the Red Cross, "as Serbs, so that they would get a good impression." Can you tell us precisely what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: This is where they slept, the Serbs who guarded us. They slept in that room. And during the day, when this inspection came, they were forewarned that the Red Cross would come. So this is why they put in Mergud [phoen], Pasaga Tihic, and a few other people in there, and made it look as though they slept on those beds. They put up a show for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And these people, Mergud, Pasaga Tihic, and the other people, were they in fact prisoners who were being detained in the TO or the SUP?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were prisoners in the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And did they report to you that they had been presented to the ICRC -- the international committee for the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. They wanted to show that these people looked well, but they were in fact their people, and it was well known.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. Now, I just want to return to another topic. You've already said that in the SUP no one told you why you had been arrested. Did anyone ever provide you with an explanation as to the reason for your arrest and detention when you were in the TO building or in the two years in which you were held in custody at Batkovici? Was it ever explained to you why you had been arrested and detained?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: No, it was never explained to me; however, I myself knew why I had been arrested, because I was a member of the SDA. People who were members of the HDZ and SDA were arrested. HDZ was the Croatian Democratic Party. SDA is the Party of Democratic Action. So that means that they hindered democracy --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: -- unlike in other countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In the TO building, just going back to the TO building, were you ever interviewed by any officials? Sorry. Not necessarily inside the TO building, but during the period of time in which you were held in custody at the TO, were you ever interviewed by officials?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was interrogated by somebody who was a former misdemeanour judge; his name is Simo Bozic. I was taken there by two people who were imprisoned with me, and he interrogated me there. There was a typist there as well. He asked me about how the SDA armed itself, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I'll just get what I need from you on this episode. First of all, I take it with the typist being there, that what you said was recorded. Am I correct or incorrect?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Was this interview on or about the 7th of July, 1992?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I'm not very accurate when it comes to the dates. I couldn't be more specific, because they took me to that building several times, to the SUP, which was across, but I can't remember the date. It all took place after the 3rd of July, when they beat me, some four to five days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. That's good enough. That's good enough for me. Thanks very much. What was the general theme of the questions?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: About the role of the SDA, about our intentions, and along those lines. I had nothing to tell them regarding that, because these were all public topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Fine. And on this occasion, did --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I completely understand the intention of my learned friend to wind up the proceedings, but just right now, this witness said it was a fact of common knowledge that all parties -- and then he was cut, cut in the explanations by my learned friend. Maybe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: At what stage was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It was just when he was answering in 79, line 9: "All public topics." And then this witness said: "It was a common known fact that all parties ..." and then he tried to explain. Maybe it might be of certain importance for this Trial Chamber to find out what he was -- what was his intention to explain, I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no. You can deal with that in cross-examination, if you think it's important for your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I mean, like before, when the witness is trying to explain something, then he should be allowed for that. That was my intention, Your Honour. Of course, we shall have time to clarify that in our cross-examination, but it was just in the midway of his explanation, he was cut by my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That's up to the Prosecution if they think it is important. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. I'm not minded to go into that. Mr. Pantelic, of course, will be free to explore that in his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, during the course of this interview, did Bozic ever give you any explanation or idea of any charge that you might have been arrested on or any charge that you might be facing?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't say anything to me. I know that others were convicted later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: But what about others?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness mentioned a name. The interpreters did not hear it. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I'm not asking about others, just you. He didn't provide you with any details of that, I take it, of any charge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The interpreters are saying a name was mentioned but they didn't get it. MR. DI FAZIO: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What was the name that you mentioned, Mr. Bobic?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: I wanted to say that everything was done in a democratic way. I didn't intend to say anything else. Simo Bozic didn't explain anything to me why I was there. He simply made the notes about what I was saying. He asked me about the SDA party, how did the process of our arming go on, how much -- how many firearms we had. I told him we had no firearms, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's go back to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Di Fazio. One -- it might be a question of translation, but in the answer, Mr. Bobic's answer on page 81, line 1, where Mr. Bobic says: "I wanted to say that everything was done in a democratic way." I'm just wondering whether that's what he actually said, and if so, what he means. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Yes. I'll clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You said in an answer just given a short moment ago that everything was done in a democratic way. What were you trying to say there?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Well, everything was democratic. We had three parties: The SDS, the HDZ, and the SDA. These parties were in the old cinema building. We had normal contacts. There were no incidents, and everything went along in a normal way, up until the 16th or 17th. We had democratic processes. We had normal communication. We would sit down and have a drink with each other. Nobody could tell that the war was going to break out. Everything was normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for clarifying that. Okay. Now let's get back to Batkovici. In the period of time that you were in Batkovici you visited by a man named Stevanovic?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. Cvijetin Stevanovic, from Loncari, the son of Krsto. MR. DI FAZIO: Can the witness be shown the very last Prosecution Exhibit, P135. Thank you very much. Perhaps it's best if we get both -- or just the B/C/S statement, actually, which is P135 ter ID at this stage.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P135? MR. DI FAZIO: 135, the most recent Prosecution Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. It was marked today, actually. MR. DI FAZIO: It's ID, marked earlier this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just something regarding the transcript. The witness said, on page 81, line 17, when he started talking, he said: "Had I known that the war was going to break out in Samac, I would have left Samac." However, this was not recorded in the transcript, so could my learned friend please clarify this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Everybody tries to flee if there is any danger of something evil. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. The witness has done the job for me. I'm grateful to you. Now let's look at the document, please, P135 ID.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Is that your signature that appears on the document?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And can you tell us of the circumstances under which you signed this power of attorney, please?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: I was in the camp, and I didn't know about things that were going on at the time --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Sorry. Before you continue, may I ask that the witness place the document on the ELMO so that the defendants and everyone else can see it? You'll have to read it, if you need, from either the TV screen in front of you or off the document itself, but it has to remain on that device on your right-hand side, Mr. Bobic, so that we can all see it. Thank you. All right. Yes. Now, the circumstances under which you came to sign it, please.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: A man who guarded us, a Serb, called Aleksandar Djuric, came to get me and told me, "Kemal, you have a visitor, and go and wash yourself." So I went and washed myself. And then we went for some 1 kilometre to a ramp where Stevanovic, the son of Krsto, was waiting for us. Aco, who was a nice man, told me along the way, "Kemal, sign the document, or otherwise you might perish." I was in the camp. It was a typical camp. So once I got there, he said, "I know this man." And then we greeted each other and he said that he came because he was not allowed to move into my house, and he took out a lot of documents showing the land registry from Samac, and one of the documents was also certified in Bijeljina, and he showed it to us. And he told me that he would move into my house and would watch over my property, and then once I came back and revoked it, it would be given back to me. However, all of my property was sold away. My house had four three-room apartments. There was also a building in the yard. I had two shops on the ground level. They were used for a shop and herbal pharmacy. There was a corridor, a very wide corridor, with a kitchen on both sides, because they were used by us two brothers. So in the middle there were vaults, and we would go back and forth from one side of the house to the other. When he moved --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... can I just ask you, though, to concentrate on what actually happened as you were standing on the ramp at the -- in Batkovici, and you signed the document? Let me ask you this: Did you feel that you had any choice as to whether or not you signed the document?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: No. One's life was worth less than an ashtray in the camp. Had I not signed it, I would have been taken away, and God knows where I would have ended. And then he asked me to read it, and I said that I couldn't see, because we spent our days in the dark in the hangar. And then I asked for a document to be shown to me. And could you give me a copy? And then this is the copy, and I have the original. I took a copy and I gave her ten marks. She didn't ask me that. It wasn't much money. I gave the money to her for coffee, and she told me, "Hold on to this, because these are hard times, but your house will be returned to you." And that's how it was in the end, but unfortunately it was not in proper condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Who was the "she" who you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: She was probably a lawyer. I don't know. She came in with the documents. I really don't know, so I can't tell you. But in light of the function that she had, the role that she played, she came with him, then went back to Bijeljina, and returned with the documents. She gave me two documents, in fact. The documents were signed also by the three women, my brother's two daughters and his wife, indicating that the house, the whole house now belonged to him. And let me just tell you about this document. We had a trial in Brcko for this, in this matter, and we won the case. He has to give me 150.000 marks plus the court expenses. I spent about 3.000 German marks for the lawyer, Slobodan Zelic ^; a Serb lawyer represented me in that case. Then we were again transferred to Brcko for the second hearing in another case. I also won everything in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: It was an inheritance hearing. And then I also went to Samac. I had a legal suit in Samac and I also won. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I don't want to go into the history of the subsequent court actions regarding the fallout, the consequences of this document. I want to know how it came to be signed. First of all, you've referred to documents signed by three women. This document that you have before you, this document here that's on the ELMO machine, that was only signed by yourself, was it not?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can put this also on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: No. No. I don't want you to do that. I'm only asking you about this particular document, Witness.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: All right. But just in case you're interested, I also have a copy of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: If Defence counsel want to ask you about it, they now know that it's in your possession there and in your bag. Okay. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: I seek to produce the document fully into evidence, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any objection from the Defence? I see none. Can we confirm the number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. It will be P135 and P135 ter. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Just one question. I'll be grateful if you would answer it very, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You say that you won -- you say that you won subsequent legal actions. Were you, in practical terms, ever able to enforce those judgements in your favour?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: No. Since now it belongs to Bosanski Samac and the court ruled in my favour, but we cannot implement it because various ways are found to avoid it. The man who robbed me, Stevanovic Cvijetin, also has a night bar, nightclub, and we are working on having this nightclub confiscated from him. But we're working on it, and so is, in fact, the chief ombudsman in Sarajevo. He's also involved in the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'll return to the question of your property briefly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Di Fazio. Just one point, line 10 of page 86. Mr. Bobic says: "Since now it belongs to Bosanski Samac." Is that a correct translation of what you said, Mr. Bobic? And if so, what belongs -- what is the "it" that belongs to Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since now, in recent times, before new -- before the New Year's day, Loncari became a part of Bosanski Samac, and he's from there, Loncari or Zabari. And the whole event in which I was robbed took place in Samac, and the Court in Samac had jurisdiction over the case, conducted that case. Milos Savic was the president of the Court in Bosanski Samac. He was the Presiding Judge and he ruled in my favour, but his decision simply cannot be implemented. And Samac is now a part of the Serb Republic. And that is impeding the whole process, and the whole process has lasted for three years now. Can you imagine that? And the decisions cannot be implemented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm not certain whether I'm that clear, but perhaps you should move on and -- MR. DI FAZIO: I think that's probably --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If I may be of assistance to Her Honour Judge Williams. Well, Your Honour, maybe it's a wrong understanding that this house and the other items belongs now to municipality of Bosanski Samac. In fact, this witness said that his case is now under the jurisdiction of the Court in Samac, which is a part of the judicial system of Republika Srpska and there is a second level in Modrica court, et cetera, et cetera. So it was not the now issue of whether the house and the other property of this witness belongs to municipality, by any way. It's simply a civil affair before the Court in Samac. I don't know if that satisfies Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. MR. DI FAZIO: I think I'll prefer to return to this topic after I've had a moment to gather my thoughts about it, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: I think it would probably be more beneficial if I was able to do that to the Chamber. And although I'm close to finishing this witness's evidence, I don't think that I will finish today. So perhaps, if I may, I may return to this topic very briefly tomorrow, if I think it's necessary, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: So may I now turn to another topic, Mr. Bobic, and that is the question of exchanges.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: From time to time, were people exchanged from Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes, some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: To bring about this process of exchange, was it necessary to pay money?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: For some, yes; for others, no. It depended on who you were. The people who were brought in from Manjaca, they were exchanged and they immediately went on to third countries, because they came to pick them up in Batkovici. I know about a case of a man from Kozarac. His brothers came and paid some money for him. He had four brothers there, and they paid money for him and he went to be exchanged. I asked him how much money it was, and he said that he didn't know. A car came to pick him up in the afternoon and he was simply driven away. I don't know who was in charge of that, who dealt with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever see any of the defendants at Batkovici apparently dealing with exchange issues?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was Mr. Miroslav Tadic. He was in Batkovici. He exchanged Jasenko Suljic and Mario Begic. He drove them away in his car. I can't say whether he took money for that or not, because I wasn't there. I didn't see. And immediately after that, Emin Gibic got out, so did Sabah Seric and Miki Tabakovic [phoen]. They also said that they would be exchanged. Now, I don't know what the reason was why they were able to leave so quickly. I don't know whether they had to give money. I cannot allege that this man took money.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Which man?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Miroslav Tadic. You asked me if anyone came there from the accused, and Miroslav Tadic was there. I know that. And he knows, because he saw me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You were eventually released from -- via an exchange in Sarajevo in 1994. Did you discuss the circumstances of that with your wife?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Well, it's hard to say. I was in the camp. My wife later told me that she had given I think 12.000 German marks to Miroslav Tadic to be exchanged, and then Mr. Tesic, son of Stjepan, came. He was supposed to come for me. And the exchange never took place in my case. And I don't know whether she did in fact give the money to him or not. I only can go by what she told me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Bobic. You mentioned, I believe, one man who was exchanged called Sabah Seric. Is that correct? I'm not sure whether I'm pronouncing his name correctly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Sabah Seric. You said it quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you. Was he the son of Hasan Seric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: And would you be able --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The shop owner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Would you be able to recall when he was exchanged, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was exchanged the very same day when Begic was driven away. That was the same day when Begic went to be exchanged in Tuzla, Bahrija Begic, and the father-in-law looked for him in Gracanica. Jasan Kosuljic [phoen], he was exchanged in Gracanica. I don't know where the exchanges took place, but that's, I think, where he was exchanged. They didn't go in that direction, the others. I don't know where they went. The people that were to be exchanged, their names were read out and then the doors would be closed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm just interested in knowing whether you can recall the month and the year, if you can. It might be helpful to us. MR. DI FAZIO: Does Your Honour mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Of Sabah Seric, son of Hasan, yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you please answer Her Honour's inquiry?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember the date, really. I know that it was in winter. But there was no snow, but it was not very cold either. Somewhere in between.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And you know it was in winter. Can you tell us if it was soon after your arrival at Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes. We came there together. Seric, myself, Jasenko, Bahrija Begic, we all came from Samac in Batkovici together. And then, in the early evening, the Croats came. They came separately, on another bus. And then the people from Manjaca came, and so on, people from Kotor Vares, Banja Luka, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes, but the question is this: You've told us that this Sabah Seric man was exchanged, you've told us it was winter. My question is: Was it soon after you arrived at Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: It may have been just before the New Year's Day, perhaps around Christmas and somewhere like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Did prisoners discuss amongst themselves ways of bringing about the exchange, their exchange?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Well, there were the exchanges, and Serbs, when they wanted an exchange to take place, when the two parties agreed about the exchange, the leader that exchanged us living human beings, then they would meet in a location, whether in the Serb territory or on the other side, and then they agree about when the exchange would take place. And then on that date, at that time, they would -- people would be exchanged. Those who were lucky would be exchanged; those who weren't lucky were not exchanged. I was not lucky.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. But the question is simple: Did prisoners, when you were locked up, locked up inside the hangars at Batkovici, discuss among themselves, prisoner to prisoner, how to get out, how to be exchanged, what to do to bring about an exchange? Did you talk about it?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, we did discuss this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And was it ever agreed that there was a particular way to bring it about?

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Well, mostly those who had money, they were exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever hear amongst prisoners talking amongst themselves who --

utterances.speaker: KEMAL BOBIC
utterances.text: Yes, but the exchange was always -- the exchange was always the main attraction, the main topic. Everybody wanted to be exchanged, because it was really difficult to be away from your family, from your children. Everybody wanted to leave as soon as possible. Some people stayed there for six months, some for a year, and I stayed there for a whole two years. I spent three winters there: 1992, 1993, and 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... being productive, are we? MR. DI FAZIO: No. I'll -- it's now 1.45. I'm going to wrap up this topic tomorrow and the other issue of property tomorrow, and I've just about come to the end of my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: How long? MR. DI FAZIO: I would say about 15, 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. MR. DI FAZIO: Possibly even less, but I'll say 20 minutes at this stage just in case things develop, but I hope to be less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. MR. DI FAZIO: Is -- there are a number of topics that I think that the Chamber wants me to address them on very briefly, but just regarding the remainder of the week. Do you want me to deal with that now or later, or tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The courtroom is required. I think we can deal with it when we have time, within our allocation of time. MR. DI FAZIO: Certainly. Then, perhaps, I'll do it tomorrow at the conclusion of this witness's evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We shall adjourn now until tomorrow at 0900 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
